summary.text: The front matter of a 2011 WHO, UNFPA, UNAIDS and IPPF case study from Swaziland on linking sexual and reproductive health with HIV/AIDS services, in support of the Global Plan to eliminate new HIV infections among children. Key definitions
In delineating the full scope of a linked SRH and HIV response, the 
following distinction has been made between linkages and integration:2 
Linkages
Bi-directional (two-way) synergies in policy, programmes, services and 
advocacy between SRH and HIV. This is a broad, human rights-based 
approach, of which service integration is a sub-set. 
Integration
Joining together different kinds of SRH and HIV services to ensure and 
maximize collective outcomes. This includes referrals from one service to 
another, aiming to off

summary.text: Defines the distinction between linkages and integration of sexual and reproductive health and HIV services, and notes a shift in global attention from preventing mother-to-child transmission alone towards recognizing links between maternal health, HIV and child survival under the Millennium Development Goals.

blocks.title: The commitment towards elimination of new HIV infections among children by 2015 and keeping their mothers alive
blocks.content:
elimination of new HIV infections 
among children by 2015 and 
keeping their mothers alive
Building on the past progress and 
success of country-led national 
PMTCT programmes, there is 
renewed global consensus that  
the world must now strive 
towards the elimination of new 
HIV infections among children 
by 2015 and keeping mothers 
alive. These joint goals can be 
achieved at a country level through 
implementation of the four prongs 
(see Table 1) for comprehensive 
programming of elimination of 
mother-to-child transmission 
(eMTCT), integrated with sexual and 
reproductive health (SRH).

summary.text: Explains the global commitment to eliminate new HIV infections among children by 2015 while keeping mothers alive, built on four prongs of comprehensive programming integrated with sexual and reproductive health. It highlights growing attention to the first two prongs, preventing HIV in women and preventing unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV. Tables set out the prongs and associated interventions such as family planning, blood safety, stigma reduction and prevention of gender-based violence.

blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Swaziland is known for having the 
highest rate of adult HIV infection 
in the world, with a recent figure 
at 25.9%.14 Swaziland is also one 
of 22 low- and middle-income 
priority countries15 with the highest 
estimated numbers of pregnant 
women living with HIV. 
The generalized HIV epidemic has 
had a devastating effect on this small 
country: its present life expectancy 
(49 years for the total population) 
is one of the lowest in the world,16 
with women and children being 
particularly affected.

summary.text: Describes the background to Swaziland's HIV epidemic, noting the world's highest adult HIV prevalence, very low life expectancy and a high proportion of pregnant women living with HIV. It closes with a statement by the Prime Minister to the UN General Assembly committing the country to reduce new infections among children to zero by 2015.

Established in 1979, the Family Life Association of Swaziland (FLAS), an 
affiliate of the International Planned Parenthood Association (IPPF), focuses 
on providing SRH services and information to young people in Swaziland. 
A range of HIV-related services, including ART, is comprehensively integrated

summary.text: Profiles the case study sites in Swaziland, starting with the Family Life Association of Swaziland and its youth-friendly clinics offering integrated sexual and reproductive health and HIV services, alongside other service providers mapped across the country. It then documents promising practices addressing Prong 1, preventing HIV among women, and Prong 2, preventing unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV. The section covers community outreach, peer education, counselling, family planning and linked referral services. It ends with a checklist of questions that facilities can use to assess whether they provide these services and have built them into standard operating procedures.
